title: How We Think
author: John Dewey
directions: Notice the difference between an idea arriving and a reason being examined. Try describing a belief without defending it. What observation led you there, and which part is an assumption? The distinction helps us read Dewey actively.

A useful question gives uncertainty a shape. Think of a situation where your first explanation felt obvious. Identify one detail that explanation leaves unexplained. The aim is not endless doubt, but a question specific enough to investigate.

Separate the observation from the step you use to interpret it. If someone disagrees, ask which of those two steps differs. A disagreement can become more productive when the evidence and the inference are visible separately.

Pay attention to the activity of learning, not just the finished answer. Describe an occasion when a small surprise led you to look more closely. What allowed that curiosity to continue, and what made it stop?

Choose one ordinary question you can examine this week. State what you expect, what you will observe, and what would surprise you. That turns a pleasing idea into an inquiry with a result you can revisit.

title: The Crowd
author: Gustave Le Bon
directions: Le Bon offers a historical theory, not a rule for judging every group. Watch for the distance between a vivid example and a universal claim. We can understand an argument without accepting all of its generalizations.

Compare the emotion surrounding a message with the information contained in it. Both matter, but they are different things. Ask what you would think about the same claim if it arrived without applause, urgency, or dramatic presentation.

A concrete image can make an idea memorable. It can also make a complicated event seem simpler than it is. Notice which detail a powerful image brings forward, and which detail disappears outside its frame.

Ask whether a statement became better supported or merely more familiar. Listen for the source of authority: a method, an observation, a reputation, or an audience reaction. Those are different reasons for believing something.

Before reading reactions, write your own question about a claim. Then use the group’s information to improve it. Independent judgment does not require ignoring other people; it requires making your reasoning available for examination.

title: The Psychology Of Revolution
author: Gustave Le Bon
directions: This is one author’s historical interpretation. Treat its dramatic categories as claims to examine. A large event contains different motives, experiences, and choices. One explanation rarely gives each participant the same amount of attention.

A belief can describe the world and also express belonging. Ask which function it is serving in a particular passage. Evidence about a claim and evidence about why people hold it answer different questions.
Look for the work done by a phrase or a symbol. What does it invite people to remember, fear, or hope for? A symbol can carry shared meaning while leaving important disagreements unresolved.

Bring the scale back to a concrete decision. Which institution sets the choices, who makes the decision, and who experiences the result? These questions resist the temptation to describe every person in a movement as interchangeable.

Choose one explanation of a historical event and name a missing perspective. Add that perspective without claiming it explains everything. Careful reading can make a story more complex while making your questions more precise.

title: Psychology: Briefer Course
author: William James
directions: Distinguish a description of an experience from an explanation of its cause. You may know that something caught your attention without knowing why it happened. That boundary makes observation more useful, not less valuable.

Notice what becomes prominent while you are absorbed in one activity. Then notice what returns when you pause. Use the example to ask how selection shapes experience, rather than assuming you take in everything around you equally.

Try describing the transitions between thoughts instead of listing isolated ideas. An interruption, a memory, or a sound can change what follows. The transitions are part of the experience you are trying to understand.

Pick one repeated action and describe the conditions that make it easy. Avoid turning the description into a fixed label about your character. A change in the first step can be easier to examine than a promise to change your whole identity.

Return to one observation and give two possible interpretations. Then ask what further information would help distinguish them. A historical text becomes a useful partner when it sharpens what you can ask about your own example.

title: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
author: Charles Darwin
directions: Begin with description. Notice a movement, a posture, or a change in the face before assigning a motive. A visible response is information, but understanding its meaning also requires context and the person’s own account.

Darwin connects some expressions with the history of useful actions. Treat the connection as an argument to examine. Ask which observations support it and which further assumptions are needed to move from a present movement to an explanation of its origin.

An opposite posture can make a contrast easy to notice. Use that contrast without imagining it gives a complete dictionary of feelings. Real situations may combine different motives and bodily responses at the same time.

Notice that feeling is not only a sentence spoken inside the mind. A response may involve breathing, tension, or movement. These observations do not diagnose someone; they remind us to describe experience with more than one kind of detail.

The practical conclusion is a better question. Instead of announcing what another person’s face means, ask what is happening for them. Observation can open a conversation. It should not close the conversation before the person has spoken.

title: Psychology and Industrial Efficiency
author: Hugo Münsterberg
directions: Münsterberg argues for bringing psychological investigation into practical settings. The historical methods require scrutiny, but the change in question is useful: what information does the actual task give us that a distant judgment would miss?

Describe the work before describing the worker. What must be noticed, remembered, or decided? Which interruptions are built into the process? This description gives a change something specific to address.

A training exercise should make its goal observable. Decide what an improvement would look like, then check whether the exercise actually helped. The purpose is to learn from the result, not to reward an impressive explanation of the method.

Historical selection methods should not be accepted uncritically. Ask what a test measures, how closely that resembles the work, and who may be disadvantaged by its assumptions. A score is not the whole person or the whole task.

Choose one source of friction in a repeated routine. Change one condition and compare the result with the earlier description. Keep the observation modest: a useful local improvement is more informative than an unsupported promise of universal efficiency.

title: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis
author: Sigmund Freud
directions: Freud presents an influential way of interpreting mental life. We are reading a historical theory, not using it to diagnose a listener. Keep the example separate from the explanation, and notice when the explanation asks you to accept more than the observation itself establishes.

An everyday error may invite several explanations. Freud’s lectures make interpretation central, but a careful reader can still ask what alternatives deserve consideration. Curiosity about a mistake does not make one dramatic explanation certain.

Distinguish the remembered description of a dream from the meanings proposed for it. An interpretation may be interesting without becoming a fact established by the dream alone. Notice which part comes from the dreamer and which part is added by an interpreter.

Ask how the method handles disagreement or an unsuccessful explanation. What would lead an investigator to revise an interpretation? This is a question about evaluating a theory, rather than an invitation to analyze a stranger’s private life.

You can understand why a work mattered without accepting every claim in it. Choose one idea you can describe fairly, one assumption you would question, and one piece of evidence you would want before reaching a stronger conclusion.

title: Dream Psychology
author: Sigmund Freud
directions: Dream Psychology presents Freud’s account of dreams and interpretation. It is an influential historical work, not a universal decoding key. The first distinction is between describing what you remember and claiming to know why it appeared.

A remembered dream is already a report made after waking. Notice which details feel clear and which have been reconstructed while telling the story. Uncertainty about a detail is useful information, not something you need to hide from the account.

An association can tell you what an image brings to mind for a person. It does not automatically establish a hidden cause. Keep a possible meaning in the form of a question when the evidence does not justify turning it into a conclusion.

A satisfying explanation can feel complete because its parts fit a story. Ask whether other explanations could fit the same details. This does not require dismissing interpretation; it requires distinguishing the pleasure of a coherent story from the strength of its support.

If you choose to reflect on a dream, separate three notes: what you remember, what it makes you think of, and what you do not know. None of those notes is a diagnosis. The exercise preserves curiosity while leaving room for uncertainty.
